paras: The mob attack on the King family was a night raid on December 30, 1881, in which an armed mob fired into the King family's cabin near Americus, in Montgomery County, Missouri, killing Mrs. Nancy Austin and wounding Mrs. King and at least one son. It came the night after one of the King brothers was shot dead while trying to force his way into a neighbor's house. The story ran nationally in January 1882 and again in March, when the family filed damage suits against members of the mob.

A St. Louis dispatch counted the King brothers among "reckless and law-defying young men" hated by the "law-abiding people" of southern Montgomery County. A Montgomery City dispatch said the brothers, tie-choppers among German settlers, broke furniture when refused liquor and were "a sort of terror to the neighborhood." No account states the race of the family or of its attackers.

On Thursday evening, December 29, Jack (or John), Joe and Tom King went to John Nelson's house near Rhineland, saying they wanted a drink. When they broke a window, Nelson fired on them; Jack King was found dead near the gate and Joe was hit with birdshot. The Nelsons said the Kings had come to rob them, which the Kings denied, and a coroner's jury exonerated Nelson. Jack King's body was taken to the family cabin, home to the elder Kings, two sons, their wives and the wives' mother, Mrs. Austin.

On Friday night a mob said to number twenty-five to fifty came to the cabin and ordered the elder King back inside. When Mrs. King and Mrs. Austin came out, "it is said," the mob began firing, and the sons fled by the back door. Mrs. Austin was killed, Mrs. King was shot twice in the leg, Joe King was shot in the abdomen, hand and arm, and Tom King was missing and hurt. A March account said one wounded son crawled a mile and a half through the snow, losing an eye and freezing his hands and feet.

Abbie King, the youngest brother, asked to be jailed at Danville for protection, and on Tuesday swore out a warrant against the unnamed mob, for which Sheriff Gregory summoned a posse. According to the Globe-Democrat's Mexico correspondent, two mob members were arrested and discharged, and local feeling favored the mob of "respectable and wealthy citizens." On March 13, 1882, Forrist & Fry of Mexico filed five damage suits in the Montgomery County Circuit Court, funded by residents' subscriptions. No report of an indictment or of the suits' outcome appears in the coverage.

A St. Louis dispatch of January 4 ran in the Memphis Public Ledger as "Two Families Engaged in a Bloody War." The Memphis Daily Appeal headed it "Kings Killed. Three Men and One Woman Murdered in Missouri." It also ran in Sacramento, Wheeling and Bismarck, and the St. Paul Daily Globe headlined it "A Gang of Reckless Desperadoes Almost Completely Destroyed by Citizens," casting the family as the outlaws. A shorter version in Savannah and Knoxville said young Nelson, not a King, died at the Nelson house.

The Montgomery City dispatch ran in the Mexico Weekly Ledger as "Three Kings. Murder and Riot" and in the Crawford Avalanche as "Exterminating a Family." By March the tone had turned against the mob: the Globe-Democrat special promised its members "Justice Meted Out," and the West-Jersey Pioneer, while calling the Kings "drunkards, brawlers, and thieves," called the raid a "dastardly and murderous deed" by "lynchers."

Accounts differ on the first death: Missouri reports named Jack King, the short wire young Nelson, and the New Jersey paragraph "a very popular young man" killed by the brothers in a bar-room fight. January reports named only Mrs. Austin as certainly killed in the raid, the short wire added a King son, and the March accounts said a son and a daughter died. The New Jersey paragraph said no prosecution was attempted, while the Missouri correspondent reported two arrests ending in discharge.

reader.title: Mob attack on the King family (Montgomery County, Missouri)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: An armed mob of citizens fired into the King family's cabin at night, killing Mrs. Nancy Austin and wounding others, a day after one of the King sons was shot at a neighbor's house; the March accounts call the attackers 'lynchers' and a 'mob' organized to 'clean out' the family (A11, A13, A14, A15).

A mob said to number 25 to 50 (or 50 or more) with no lawful authority killed Mrs. Austin and possibly a King son (A11, A13, A14); it acted against a family the press called 'law-defying' after the alleged break-in at Nelson's, and A15 names the attackers 'lynchers' (A2, A15). The person certainly killed was not herself accused of anything, and no paper states anyone's race.

A St. Louis wire (A2), a separate Montgomery City dispatch (A11, A13) and a later Globe-Democrat special from Mexico, Mo. (A14) agree that a mob fired on the King cabin and killed Mrs. Austin, though they differ on other casualties.

accounts.label: St. Louis wire (Jan. 4)
accounts.gist: The King boys, 'law-defying' young men, went to Nelson's house, the Nelsons said to rob it; one King was killed; next night a 'band of citizens bent on the destruction of the Kings' attacked the cabin, killing Mrs. Austin and wounding Mrs. King and a son.

accounts.label: Short St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: Young Nelson was killed in the fight at his house; on Saturday, December 31, citizens killed Mrs. Austin and another King son and wounded Mrs. King and a son.

accounts.label: Montgomery City dispatch
accounts.gist: Drunken King brothers broke a window at Nellison's; he shot Jack dead; a coroner's jury exonerated him; Friday night a mob of 25 to 50 fired on the cabin, killing Mrs. Austin and wounding Mrs. King and Joe King.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat Mexico correspondent (March)
accounts.gist: Citizens organized a mob to 'clean out' the family; fifty or more fired volleys into the house about midnight, killing a son and a daughter and wounding the mother and a son; two arrests ended in discharge; five damage suits were filed.

accounts.label: New Jersey editorial (March)
accounts.gist: The Kings killed a popular young man in a bar-room fight at Christmas; masked men killed a son and daughter next night; the influential 'lynchers' went unprosecuted until money was raised for suits.

framing.detail: The St. Louis wire cast the Kings among 'reckless and law-defying young men' hated by 'law-abiding people' while headlining 'Kings Killed. Three Men and One Woman Murdered' and calling the raid a 'frightful tragedy'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined 'Missouri Marauders. A Gang of Reckless Desperadoes Almost Completely Destroyed by Citizens'.
The Mexico Weekly Ledger ran the Montgomery City dispatch as 'Three Kings. Murder and Riot in Montgomery County', with 'it is said' hedging on who fired first.
The Globe-Democrat special headed 'The Montgomery County Mob' expected 'Justice Meted Out' to the mob of 'respectable and wealthy citizens'.
The West-Jersey Pioneer called the Kings 'drunkards, brawlers, and thieves' but the raid a 'dastardly and murderous deed' by 'lynchers' and 'assassins'.
